picked.t: 푸꾸옥, ‘렌터카업체’ 관리감독 강화키로…올 들어 외국인 연루 교통사고 잇따라
picked.body: 움주운전 여부를 확인 중인 푸꾸옥 교통경찰. (사진=안장성 공안국) 베트남 대표 휴양섬 푸꾸옥 당국이 렌터카에 대한 관리·감독을 강화한다. 올 들어 외국인이 대여 차량을 직접 몰다 발생한 교통사고가 잇따른 데 따른 영향이다. 푸꾸옥을 관할하는 안장성(An Giang)의 응우옌 하이 즈엉(Nguyen Hai Duong) 공안국 자문부서장은 최근 브리핑을 통해 이 같은 방침을 밝혔다. 즈엉 부서장은 “올해 초부터 외국인이 대여 차량을 직접 운전하다 낸 교통사고는 모두 4건으로, 사고에 연루된 운전자 중 3명은 운전면허가 없는 상태였다”고 밝혔다. 올 들어 외국인이 대여 차량을 운전하다 발생하는 사고가 잇따르자 당국은 푸꾸옥 내 주요 렌터카·이륜차 대여 업체 5곳으로부터 교통 안전 규정 준수에 대한 서약서를 받는 등 자동차·이륜차 대여 업체에 대한 점검 및 단속을 강화했다. 즈엉 부서장은 “렌터카 및 이륜차 대여 업체는 이용객의 신분증과 운전면허를 확인해야 하며, 면허가 베트남에서 인정되는지와 대여하려는 차종에 유효한지도 확인해야 한다”며 “외국인 관광객의 면허 발급국과 유효기간, 허용 차종을 확인하고 위반 사항은 규정에 따라 엄중 처리하겠다”고 말했다. 이와 함께 당국은 푸꾸옥 관광객 안전을 높이기 위한 노력의 일환으로 △면허 요건 △헬멧 착용 △속도 제한 등 교통 규정을 알리는 인식 제고 활동도 강화하는 한편, 즈엉동(Duong Dong)과 안터이(An Thoi), 끄어깐(Cua Can), 끄어즈엉(Cua Duong), 간저우(Ganh Dau) 등 주요 관광지와 항구·공항·리조트·관광지를 잇는 도로에서 순찰·단속을 강화했다.

호치민시 껀저와 붕따우 지역 간 해상교 및 해저터널 경로. (조감도=TEDI) 베트남 호치민시 껀저(Can Gio)와 붕따우(Vung Tau) 지역을 잇는 해상교 건축안의 설계공모 당선작이 발표되면서 본 사업에 대한 기대감이 높아지고 있다. 호치민시 인민위원회는 최근 껀저-붕따우 해상교 건축안 설계공모 결과를 승인했다. 심사위원회 채점 결과, 교통운송설계자문총공사(TEDI)가 제출한 출품번호 ‘VB02’가 88.11점을 획득하며 1등으로 당선됐다. 당국에 따르면, 1등으로 당선된 건축안은 설계 개선 과정을 거쳐 이후 사업 단계의 기초로 활용된다. 호치민시 인민위원회는 당선작 출품 업체가 심사위원회의 의견에 따라 최종 설계안을 구체화할 수 있도록 지도하기 위해 심사위원회 및 시 기획건축국과의 협력을 사업시행자인 껀저도시관광(Can Gio Urban Tourism)에 지시했다. 이번 사업은 바다를 가로질러 호치민시 껀저와 붕따우를 잇는 총연장 약 14.1km의 해상교·해저터널 건설을 골자로 한다. 앞서 호치민시 인민의회가 지난 6월 승인한 투자정책에 따르면, 해당 사업은 민관협력사업(PPP) 건설·양도(BT) 방식으로 추진된다. 총사업비는 93조150억 동(약 36억2,860만 달러) 상당으로, 공사기간은 2026년부터 2029년까지다. 사업기간은 7년간으로, 대금은 사업 완료 및 국가 인계 후 3년에 걸쳐 지급될 예정이다. 이번 사업은 호치민시와 붕따우 지역의 연결성 개선을 통해 지역 사회경제적 발전과 해안 도시, 물류, 관광 발전 촉진하고, 호치민시 해안도로와 롱선(Long Son)산업단지 진입로를 연결해 51번 국도의 통행량 분담, 물류·항만 회랑 개발 등을 목표로 한다. 호치민시는 겐라이만(Ghenh Rai灣)을 가로지르는 해상교가 건축적 상징물로 자리매김해 지역 관광객 유치와 홍보에도 도움이 될 것으로 기대하고 있다. 현재 호치민시 껀저와 붕따우 지역을 잇는 육로는 동나이를 우회하는 51번 국도와 호치민시-롱탄-저우저이 고속도로 등에 크게 의존하고 있어, 해상교가 완공되면 이동시간이 대폭 단축됨은 물론, 기존 도로망의 부담이 크게 완화돼 지역 간 연계가 크게 강화될 것으로 기대를 모은다. 호치민시 역시 해상교 완공 시 껀저와 붕따우, 까이멥-티바이(Cai Mep-Thi Vai)항만 클러스터, 롱선 지역이 이어져 해양 관광과 물류·항만서비스·해안경제가 활성화될 것으로 기대하고 있다.

picked.t: Discover southern Vietnam through Ba Den Mountain, Cu Chi and Trang Bang
picked.body: The route starts at Cu Chi, where an underground tunnel network preserves traces of wartime life, continues through Trang Bang and ends at Ba Den Mountain, a pilgrimage destination associated with the worship of Linh Son Thanh Mau. Exploring wartime history at Cu Chi Tunnels About 70 kilometers from downtown HCMC, the Cu Chi Tunnels offer a glimpse into how local residents and soldiers lived and operated underground during the war. The historical site has two visitor areas, Ben Duoc and Ben Dinh. Travelers heading to Tay Ninh in the afternoon can spend the morning exploring either site. A guided tour at Ben Duoc takes about two hours. The underground network once housed kitchens, meeting rooms, medical facilities and other spaces, illustrating how people adapted to difficult conditions during wartime. Some sections are narrow and have low ceilings. Visitors uncomfortable with confined spaces can instead explore the above-ground exhibits. A visit often ends with boiled cassava served with sesame salt, a food associated with wartime life in Cu Chi. During food shortages, cassava was an important source of sustenance and sometimes replaced rice. Discovering Trang Bang cuisine and Ba Den Mountain From Cu Chi, travelers can stop in Trang Bang for lunch before continuing to Ba Den Mountain. Trang Bang is known for its dew-dried rice paper, typically served with boiled pork, fresh herbs and wild vegetables. Its soft, chewy texture makes it suitable for wrapping without soaking. Another local specialty is banh canh Trang Bang noodle soup. Visitors can then head to Ba Den Mountain, which rises 986 meters above sea level. The mountain is both a tourist attraction and a religious destination, with Ba Pagoda on its slopes and a Buddhist complex at the summit. Cable cars serve both areas through the Chua Hang and Tam An routes. Visitors planning to see both in one afternoon should check operating hours and the final departures. For local residents, visiting the mountain is also part of a longstanding tradition known as di vieng Ba , or paying respects to Linh Son Thanh Mau. The female deity is worshipped at Dien Ba, a shrine beside Ba Pagoda, where families offer incense and pray for health, peace and well-being. Visitors to the pagoda and shrine are encouraged to dress respectfully, with shoulders and knees covered. At the summit, the Buddhist complex features several large sculptures, including a 72-meter bronze statue of Tay Bo Da Son Bodhisattva, a Maitreya Bodhisattva statue assembled from 6,688 sandstone blocks, and a statue of Kanakamuni Buddha, one of the Buddhas of the past. The three figures represent Buddhist teachings and symbolism associated with the past, present and future. The summit also offers panoramic views of Tay Ninh's surrounding plains, with clouds sometimes gathering around the mountain. Cultural activities scheduled for November Visitors traveling to Ba Den Mountain in November can also take part in a series of cultural events and workshops. A wood sculpture exhibition titled "Moc Thien" is scheduled to open on Nov. 15 at Dieu Nghia Lecture Hall in the Ba Pagoda area. The exhibition will feature Buddhist-themed works by Venerable Thich Nu Dieu Man, head of Quan Am Pagoda on the mountain, and Buddhist followers. From Nov. 20 to 29, visitors to the summit can participate in pottery-making, painting, and calligraphy workshops. The Ba Den Leaf Market will take place on Nov. 21-22, from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m., at the food court square. Under the theme "Three Regions," the market will introduce dishes from northern, central, and southern Vietnam. Instead of paying with cash, visitors will exchange leaves for food, following a symbolic trading practice inspired by traditional local markets. The mountain's cable car operator also plans promotional fares for the year-end period. A combined ticket for the Van Son Peak and Chua Hang routes is expected to cost VND250,000 (US$9.72) from Nov. 20 to 29, a proposed 62% discount from the regular fare. A second promotion is planned for Dec. 19-31, when tickets are expected to cost VND200,000, or 69% below the regular fare. The promotional prices are subject to confirmation. Visitors should check the latest fares, operating schedules and booking conditions before traveling. The route from Cu Chi to Ba Den Mountain brings together wartime history, local food and religious traditions, offering visitors a varied journey through southern Vietnam.

picked.t: Vietnam cancer deaths surge 2.4-fold in 5 years, lung cancer leads fatalities
picked.body: In the 2021-2025 period, there were 152,100 cancer deaths, or 8.4% of all disease-related fatalities, according to a report released by the General Statistics Office on Nov. 12. The number of cancer deaths has risen steadily over the years. In 2021, 19,000 people died, or around 5% of all disease-related deaths. The figure climbed to 25,800 in 2023, or 7.3%, and to 46,800 in 2025, or 15.2%. The share of cancer deaths too increased, in fact more than tripled. The trend reveals the growing burden of cancer mortality in Vietnam. The deaths are concentrated among middle-aged and older people, with the rate rising sharply from age 40, peaking at 32.9% among those aged 60-69 before declining in the over-80 age group. However, cancer deaths among younger people have been increasing. Over the five-year period, the number of deaths in the under-20 demographic rose by more than 1.7 times, highlighting the need for greater attention to cancer monitoring, early detection, and treatment among younger age groups. Twice as many men as women died in those five years, with the proportion remaining relatively stable through the period. Lung cancer tops causes of cancer deaths Lung, liver, stomach, and colorectal cancers were the four leading killers, accounting for just over half of all cancer deaths. Lung cancer was first at 22%, followed by liver, stomach, and colorectal cancers. Associate Professor Do Hung Kien, deputy director of Hanoi's K Hospital, a leading cancer hospital in northern Vietnam, said lung cancer is a malignant disease caused by abnormal changes in the epithelial cells of the alveoli and bronchi. The disease is classified into two main types: small-cell lung cancer, which accounts for 15% of cases, and non-small-cell lung cancer, which makes up the rest. The hospital receives around 12,000 visits related to lung tumors annually on average and treats approximately 3,200 patients. "Most patients are diagnosed at stages when surgery is no longer possible, resulting in poor survival prospects," Kien said. He pointed out that, in the early stages, lung cancer often shows no symptoms, but even if it does, it could be mistaken for other respiratory conditions. It is thus frequently diagnosed only at an advanced stage, when patients develop respiratory symptoms, chest wall invasion, compression syndromes, or metastases in the brain, bones, lymph nodes, and skin. Five-year survival rates depend largely on the stage of diagnosis. They can exceed 90% for stage 1 lung cancer but fall to around 10% by stage 4, and sometimes below 1%. Experts say differences in disease patterns in various countries contribute to variations in cancer mortality rates. Professor Le Van Quang, director of K Hospital, said breast and prostate cancers are the most common in Australia, and stomach, thyroid, and colorectal cancers in South Korea. These cancers generally have better prognoses and higher survival rates, with thyroid cancer being almost entirely curable in many cases, he said. On the other hand, the lung, liver, and stomach cancers that are most common in Vietnam tend to have poor prognoses and high mortality rates, he said. He too said, many patients seek medical attention only at advanced stages when doctors can no longer perform interventions and are limited to providing palliative care, adding this is one of the reasons cancer mortality is high in Vietnam. Experts said controlling risk factors such as smoking, air pollution, and hepatitis virus infections, while improving early detection, are crucial to reducing the fatalities.

picked.t: Australian, European tourists jiggle, hug bowls of hot rice to keep warm as cold snap hits northern Vietnam
picked.body: Two clips capturing the moments, filmed on Nov. 10 by 28-year-old tour guide Ngo Quang Hieu have racked up nearly half a million views and over 30,000 likes. He recorded the footage between 3-4 p.m. and 7-8 p.m. while leading a group of 10 European and Australian travelers on a four-day, three-night tour through the northern highlands. In one, a shivering man in a jacket and shorts at Tu San Canyon can be seen jiggling nonstop, a lighthearted moment Hieu could not resist filming. The group had arrived on Nov. 9, when the weather was still warm, and so had not brought winter clothes. So, when temperatures suddenly plunged to 8-9 degrees and steady rain began to fall, everyone was caught off guard. Local stalls between Tu San Canyon and Pa Vi Village quickly ran out of gloves and scarves. "They told me winters back home bring snow and sub-zero temperatures, but it is dry cold," Hieu said. "Vietnam's damp, biting chill left them trembling." By dinnertime in Pa Vi Village, guests were wrapping homestay bath towels around their shoulders, layering extra pants and raincoats, and using both hands to hold onto steaming bowls of rice for warmth. The videos drew hundreds of comments from viewers familiar with the sting of northern Vietnam's winter. This is not the first time foreign visitors have been taken aback by the region's cold. In December 2025, a clip of two New Zealanders shivering over drinks in Tuyen Quang had gone viral. Many travelers admit they underestimated how cold it gets in Vietnam's northern mountains when packing for their trip. Tuyen Quang and neighboring provinces are currently seeing their first major cold snap of the winter, just as buckwheat flowers reach peak bloom on the Dong Van Karst Plateau, drawing large crowds of visitors. Thuat Nguyen, CEO of Mapileng Horizon Travel in Ha Giang 2 Ward, said visitors should pack thick coats, thermal layers, scarves, beanies, gloves, and sturdy shoes with good grip. Gusty winds along high mountain passes like Ma Pi Leng can make it feel even colder, and so travelers should always check the forecast and dress warmly, even if the sun is out, he added.
